Prudnik Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Prudnik, Poland

Demolished. Jews are first recorded in Prudnik in 1350, numbering 25 by 1524. A synagogue was built in 1540 and this cemetery established a year later, but rising trade conflicts, pogroms, and antisemitism led to the community's expulsion in 1570. Jews returned only after Prussia's 1812 Emancipation Edict, reaching 2.3% (126) of the population by 1840; financier Samuel Fränkel and his partners were prominent local benefactors. Kristallnacht (1938) burned the synagogue and forced the Fränkel family's textile factory into Nazi 'Aryanization'; only 79 Jews remained by 1939. A 1940 forced labor camp preceded 1942 deportations to Zagłębie Dąbrowskie ghettos. In January 1945, a death march from Auschwitz-Birkenau passed through Prudnik, with many prisoners shot; 27 exhumed victims were later reburied in the town's newer Jewish cemetery. This original cemetery, established in 1541 on land known as Sand Mountain, operated only until the 1570 expulsion.
